content.text: A heron stood so still at the tide line that I mistook it twice for a post before it proved me wrong. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it.

The reed-cutter's daughter inherits calluses before she inherits opinions, which her mother considers the correct order. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening.

Water in the channel runs brown after rain and clears again within a day, patient in a way I have never managed. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon.

We counted the nests each spring not from affection alone but because the count told us the season's temper. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone.

A basket of cut reed weighs more wet than it looks, a lesson every apprentice learns exactly once. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely.

The marsh keeps its own calendar, indifferent to the one pinned above my mother's stove. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle.

By June the reed bed stands taller than I do, and I have stopped minding being the smaller thing in the field. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become.

A fox crossed the causeway at dusk with a bird in its mouth, unhurried, as though it had every right to it. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits.

My mother taught me the difference between a reed worth cutting and one worth leaving, though she never explained why. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none.

The tide came in twice a day and asked nothing of us except that we remember to leave before it arrived. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved.

Nesting season ends the way most seasons end here, gradually, and then all at once in a single warm week. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important.

A reed-cutter's hands are read like a ledger by anyone who knows what they are looking at. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it.

The marsh in April is the only season I have ever wanted to write down exactly as it happened. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.

We sold the reed to the thatchers upriver, who complained about the price every year and paid it every year regardless. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it.

A heron's patience is the closest thing to a lesson the marsh ever offered me outright. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count.

My mother's calluses were, she said, the only inheritance she could guarantee would still be useful in fifty years. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference.

By the last cutting of the season the light goes long and gold across the water, and I have never once cut faster for it. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why.

The marsh in April smells of mud and green things deciding, finally, to commit to growing. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much.

Nesting season arrives before the birds do, in the sense that the reeds seem to know it first. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness.

My mother cut reeds the way her mother had, at the wrist and not the elbow, so the bed would recover by June. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring.

A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does.

The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished.

A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be.

The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time.

An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument.

The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing.
